n: Moroni introduces a sermon his father Mormon once gave in a Nephite synagogue. Its theme — faith, hope, and charity — makes it one of the most treasured discourses in the Book of Mormon.

f.w: faith, hope, and charity
synagogue
f.g: a building for worship and teaching; the Nephites used the word much as the Jews of Jesus’ day did.

n: Mormon begins humbly: he speaks only because God has graciously called him. This is likely before the final wars, when Mormon still led and taught the church.

f.w: the gift of his calling unto me

n: Mormon addresses faithful church members, calling them “peaceable followers of Christ.” They have enough hope to enter the Lord’s rest now — a peace in this life that continues into heaven.

f.w: peaceable followers of Christ
f.g: disciples whose lives are marked by peace — with God and with others.

f.w: the rest of the Lord

n: Mormon explains how he knows they are faithful: their peaceful way of living with others shows it. Our everyday conduct reveals our discipleship.

f.w: peaceable walk
f.g: “walk” is a scriptural way of saying one’s manner of life.

n: He quotes Jesus’ teaching that people are known by their fruits. Good works come from a good heart, just as good fruit comes from a good tree.

f.w: by their works ye shall know them

n: Mormon teaches that motive matters. A gift or prayer offered without sincere intent brings no spiritual benefit, because God looks on the heart.

f.w: real intent
f.g: sincere, honest purpose — meaning what one does.

n: An insincere act is not credited to a person as righteousness. God does not simply tally outward actions; he weighs why we do them.

f.w: counted unto him for righteousness

n: A gift given grudgingly is, in God’s eyes, as if it had never been given at all. True generosity comes from a willing heart.

f.w: grudgingly

n: The same applies to prayer. Going through the motions without sincere desire profits nothing, for God does not accept empty words.

f.w: not with real intent of heart

n: Mormon sums up: a person committed to evil cannot truly do good or give a good gift. The heart must change for the actions to become good.

f.w: a man being evil cannot do that which is good

n: Using an image from James, Mormon says a bitter spring cannot produce sweet water. No one can serve both Christ and the devil at once; following Christ means choosing a side.

f.w: a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water
cannot follow Christ

n: Everything good comes from God, and everything evil from the devil, who constantly fights God and tempts people to sin. This sets up the simple test Mormon is about to give.

f.w: all things which are good cometh of God
enticeth
f.g: lures or tempts; draws someone along by appealing to their desires.

n: Whatever invites and encourages us to do good, love God, and serve him is inspired by God. This is a key that lets anyone recognize divine influence.

f.w: every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good

n: Mormon warns against mixing things up — calling evil good or good evil. Confusing the two is a serious spiritual danger.

f.w: judge that which is evil to be of God

n: God has given us the ability to judge between good and evil, and the way is as clear as the difference between day and night. Discernment is not reserved for the few.

f.w: as the daylight is from the dark night
f.g: a vivid comparison: the difference is meant to be obvious, not subtle.

n: The “Spirit of Christ” — also called the Light of Christ — is given to every person born into the world. Anything that persuades us to do good and believe in Christ comes from him.

f.w: the Spirit of Christ is given to every man

n: The opposite is just as clear: anything that leads people to do evil, doubt Christ, or stop serving God comes from the devil. He never persuades anyone to do good.

f.w: he persuadeth no man to do good

n: Since they know this light of Christ, they must judge carefully and fairly. Echoing Jesus, Mormon reminds them that we will be judged by the standard we use on others.

f.w: with that same judgment which ye judge ye shall also be judged

n: Mormon pleads with them to search diligently by Christ’s light and to embrace every good thing. Those who do become children of Christ.

f.w: lay hold upon every good thing
a child of Christ

n: Mormon asks a question that turns the sermon toward faith: how can anyone actually take hold of every good thing?
His answer is faith. Mormon now begins the first of his three great themes, explaining how faith connects us to all good.
God, who knows all things, sent angels to announce Christ’s coming long before his birth. Every good thing would come through Christ.

f.w: he sent angels to minister unto the children of men
from everlasting to everlasting

n: God also spoke directly to prophets, testifying that Christ would come. All the prophets have borne this witness.

f.w: God also declared unto prophets

n: God made good things known in many ways. Because humankind is fallen, no good could reach us at all without Christ.

f.w: divers
otherwise men were fallen

n: Through angels and God’s word, people before Christ’s birth began to have faith in him and so received every good thing. Faith in the coming Christ was the path to salvation in every age.

f.w: every word which proceeded forth out of the mouth of God

n: After Christ came, people were still saved by faith in his name and became God’s sons and daughters. Mormon quotes Jesus’ promise that good things asked of the Father in faith will be granted.

f.w: they become the sons of God
Whatsoever thing ye shall ask the Father in my name

n: Mormon asks: now that Christ has ascended to sit at God’s right hand, have miracles stopped? Christ in heaven claims the right to extend mercy to all of us.

f.w: sat down on the right hand of God
his rights of mercy

n: Christ fully satisfied the demands of justice and now claims everyone who believes in him. He is our Advocate, pleading our cause with the Father forever.

f.w: answered the ends of the law
f.g: satisfied the purposes and demands of the law of justice.

f.w: advocateth
f.g: pleads on behalf of, as a lawyer defends a client.

n: Mormon answers his own question firmly: no, miracles have not ceased, and angels still minister to people. God’s power did not end with Bible times.

f.w: neither have angels ceased to minister

n: Angels serve under Christ’s direction and appear to those of strong faith and steady minds. Their ministry is tied to faith and godliness.

f.w: a firm mind

n: Angels call people to repentance, help fulfill God’s covenants, and teach Christ’s word to chosen servants so they can testify of him. The Restoration itself began with such ministry.

f.w: chosen vessels of the Lord
f.g: people God chooses as instruments to carry his message.

f.w: the work of the covenants of the Father

n: Through these chosen witnesses, everyone else can come to faith in Christ and make room for the Holy Ghost in their hearts. In this way the Father fulfills his covenants.

f.w: the residue of men
f.g: the rest of humanity — those who hear through the witnesses.

f.w: that the Holy Ghost may have place in their hearts

n: Mormon quotes Christ’s promise: those with faith in him can do whatever is needed and right in his eyes. “Expedient in me” means what fits Christ’s will and purposes.

f.w: expedient
f.g: appropriate, wise, or useful for a purpose.

f.w: ye shall have power to do whatsoever thing is expedient in me

n: Here is Christ’s universal invitation: everyone, everywhere, should repent, come to him, be baptized, and have faith to be saved. It is a summary of his doctrine.

f.w: Repent all ye ends of the earth

n: Mormon reasons: if these teachings are true — and God will prove them true at the last day — then how could miracles possibly have ceased?

f.w: with power and great glory at the last day

n: He presses further: have angels stopped appearing, or the Holy Ghost been withdrawn? Will God ever withhold these while even one person remains to be saved?

f.w: so long as time shall last

n: No — miracles and angels come by faith. If they ever seem to cease, it is because of unbelief, not because God has changed.

f.w: it is by faith that miracles are wrought
wo be unto the children of men

n: Since salvation comes only through faith in Christ, the end of miracles would mean the end of faith — and humanity would be as lost as if Christ had never redeemed us.

f.w: as though there had been no redemption made

n: Mormon expresses confidence in his listeners: their meekness shows they have faith in Christ. Faith is what qualifies someone to belong to his church.

f.w: I judge better things of you

n: Mormon turns to his second theme, hope, and links it tightly to faith: you cannot have one without the other.

f.w: concerning hope

n: What is the hope? Not wishful thinking, but confident expectation that through Christ’s atonement and resurrection we will be raised to eternal life.

f.w: hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection

n: Faith and hope always go together. Faith in Christ produces hope, and without faith there is nothing to hope for.
Both faith and hope require meekness and lowliness of heart — teachable humility before God.

f.w: meek, and lowly of heart
f.g: gentle, humble, and willing to submit to God.

n: God accepts only the meek and humble. Anyone who is humble and testifies by the Holy Ghost that Jesus is the Christ will also have charity — and without charity, a person is nothing.

f.w: confesses by the power of the Holy Ghost that Jesus is the Christ
if he have not charity he is nothing

n: Mormon describes charity almost word for word as Paul does in 1 Corinthians 13: patient, kind, not envious or proud, not selfish, slow to anger, enduring all things. The near-identical wording suggests a shared source in the Savior’s teaching.

f.w: charity suffereth long
puffed up
suffereth long
f.g: is patient; bears with others for a long time.

n: Charity never fails. Everything else will eventually pass away, so Mormon urges us to hold fast to charity, the greatest gift of all.

f.w: charity never faileth
cleave

n: Mormon defines charity: it is the pure love of Christ — both Christ’s love for us and the Christlike love we come to feel. Whoever has it at the last day will be well.

f.w: the pure love of Christ

n: Charity is a gift we must pray for with all the energy of our hearts. Those filled with it become God’s children, will be like Christ when he appears, and are purified as he is pure.

f.w: pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart
when he shall appear we shall be like him
